report:
## Conclusion

Your claim is **mostly false**: evidence supports tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), started late in pregnancy, as reducing hepatitis-B mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) among women with high HBV DNA—*in addition to*, not instead of, prompt newborn hepatitis-B vaccine and (where used) hepatitis-B immune globulin (HBIG).

A pivotal randomized trial in highly viremic mothers found TDF from 30–32 weeks reduced infant HBV infection at 28 weeks postpartum from **18% without maternal TDF to 5% with it**. All infants received HBIG and vaccination, so the result addresses the added value over infant prophylaxis.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa1508660

There is an important qualification. A later placebo-controlled trial (TDF begun at 28 weeks) found **no statistically demonstrable additional benefit** when infant prophylaxis was delivered extremely effectively and on time: transmission was already very rare. Thus, that trial does not show TDF is ineffective; it shows the incremental benefit can be difficult to detect when baseline risk after neonatal prevention is near zero.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1708131

The totality of evidence—including a systematic review/meta-analysis—supports peripartum antiviral prophylaxis, and the review’s authors specifically state their results support WHO’s recommendation of pregnancy TDF for prevention of HBV MTCT.  
https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laninf/article/PIIS1473-3099(20)30586-7/fulltext

The practical evidence-based interpretation is: high maternal viral load creates residual transmission risk despite infant immunoprophylaxis; late-pregnancy TDF lowers maternal HBV DNA and usually lowers that residual risk. It should be individualized by an obstetric/hepatitis specialist, rather than replacing infant vaccination/HBIG.
